title: Breadth-first search
summary: Explore a graph in rings with a queue, and find shortest paths through a grid.

steps.title: Explore in rings
body: **Breadth-first search** (BFS) visits the start, then everything 1 edge away, then everything 2 edges away, and so on, like ripples on a pond.
It is level-order traversal for graphs, plus one addition: graphs have cycles, so keep a `visited` set and never enqueue a vertex twice.
Watch the queue and `dist` in the trace. `dist[v]` is set when `v` is **first discovered**, one more than the vertex that found it.

steps.prompt: BFS from vertex 0, printing each vertex as it is dequeued. What does it print?
steps.explain: 0's neighbours are listed as 3 then 1, so they are enqueued in that order. Then 3 discovers 4, and 1 discovers 2. Finally 4 finds 5 (2 would have found it too, but it is already seen).

steps.prompt: Why does BFS mark a vertex as seen when it is **enqueued**, not when it is dequeued?
options: Otherwise the same vertex can be enqueued many times by different neighbours
It makes the queue sort itself
It does not matter at all
steps.explain: Two vertices in the same ring may both point at `v`. Marking on enqueue guarantees each vertex enters the queue once, keeping BFS `O(V + E)`.

steps.title: Shortest paths in a grid
body: In an **unweighted** graph, BFS finds shortest paths for free: a vertex is first reached through the fewest possible edges, because every closer vertex was dequeued earlier.
A maze is a graph in disguise: each open cell is a vertex joined to its up/down/left/right neighbours. Number cell `(r, c)` as `r * cols + c` so `dist` can be a plain array.
Watch the distances spread out from `S`. The wall cell is never entered, so its distance stays `-1`.

code: int r = cell / cols, c = cell % cols;
int nr = r + dr[d], nc = c + dc[d];
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) continue;

steps.prompt: The same BFS on a wider maze. `E` is the bottom-left cell. What does it print?
code: int r = cell / cols, c = cell % cols;
int nr = r + dr[d], nc = c + dc[d];
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) continue;
steps.explain: The only gap in the wall is in column 2: right, right, down, down, left, left. Six moves.
Seed the queue with the start (marked as seen), then dequeue, look at neighbours, and enqueue the unseen ones.

steps.title: BFS order
prompt: Write `List<int> BfsOrder(List<int>[] graph, int start)`: the vertices in the order BFS **dequeues** them, visiting neighbours in list order. Vertices that cannot be reached from `start` are left out.
template: var dojoSplit = new List<int>[] { new() { 1 }, new() { 0 }, new() { 3 }, new() { 2 } };
Dojo.Eq("unreachable vertices are left out", new List<int> { 2, 3 }, BfsOrder(dojoSplit, 2));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < dojoN; dojoI++) dojoLine[dojoI] = new List<int>();
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI + 1 < dojoN; dojoI++) { dojoLine[dojoI].Add(dojoI + 1); dojoLine[dojoI + 1].Add(dojoI); }
hints: Mark the start as seen and enqueue it.
Each dequeued vertex goes into `order`; then enqueue each unseen neighbour, marking it seen straight away.

steps.title: Escape the maze
prompt: Write `int ShortestPath(string[] grid)`: the fewest up/down/left/right moves from `S` to `E`, or `-1` if `E` cannot be reached. `#` is a wall; every other character is open. `S` and `E` can be anywhere.
solution: if (grid[r][c] == 'S') { dist[r * cols + c] = 0; queue.Enqueue(r * cols + c); }
int cr = cell / cols, cc = cell % cols;
int nr = cr + dr[d], nc = cc + dc[d];
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) continue;
template: if (dojoR % 2 == 1) { for (var dojoC = 0; dojoC < 400; dojoC++) dojoSb[dojoC] = '#'; dojoSb[dojoR % 4 == 1 ? 399 : 0] = '.'; }
hints: Find `S` first and start the BFS there. Number cells `r * cols + c`.
Return `dist[cell]` as soon as you dequeue the `E` cell. If the queue empties first, return -1.
